newsitem.title: PERU: Peru rescuers dig for 150 feared buried in mud.
newsitem.headline: Peru rescuers dig for 150 feared buried in mud.

text.p: Peruvian rescue workers dug through mud on Wednesday looking for at least 150 villagers feared buried after an Andean mountainside collapsed and swept away two villages.
Officials said 33 bodies had already been found after the villages of Ccocha and Pumaranra in southeast Peru were buried under a torrent of mud and rocks before dawn on Tuesday.
Villagers had been evacuated after weekend flooding but their refuge in a fold of the mountain above the village put them in the path of the mudslide.

As President Alberto Fujimori prepared to fly to the area, Civil Defence chief Gen. Homero Nurena arrived in the nearby city of Cuzco to direct operations assisted by 300 soldiers, and to evacuate other villages threatened by heavy seasonal rains.
"We are going to be evacuating people from the area who are in danger," Nurena told Reuters on arrival at Cuzco airport.

Authorities in Abancay, capital of the stricken Apurimac department, said 33 deaths were confirmed by the time darkness, fog and further small landslides forced rescuers to call off the search for more bodies under the mud late on Tuesday.

Abancay fire service Capt. Felix Vivanco Velasquez said operations were being slowed down by fog but firemen, soldiers, police and volunteers had begun their grim task. "There could be 150 to 180 bodies buried under the mud," he told Reuters.

Two other nearby villages, Kerapata and San Jorge, have also been evacuated because of the risk of mudslides and Abancay has been put on alert because of the threat of collapse of snowfields in high mountains above the city.

"The snowfield has been cracking and if that continues we have to assume there could be further mudslides that would affect the city of Abancay directly," said Mayor Luis Barra Pacheco late on Tuesday.

Rescue workers pulled dozens of bodies from the mud, many of them mutilated by the rocks swept along in the torrent. "There were arms, heads, pieces of bodies sticking out of the mud," said one firefighter. "We have tried to dig up the bodies using picks and shovels, but it's been difficult."

The Plaza de Armas square of the nearby town of Tamburco became a makeshift morgue for 24 of the victims and distraught relatives, all of them from poor farming families, begged local authorities for coffins to bury their dead.

"All my family has died, my father, my mother and my five brothers and sisters," one tearful woman told local radio. "We camped in a place high up which we thought was safe but it was swept away and they're all dead."
Civil Defence was sending 18 tonnes of supplies including food and blankets to the region as well as three dogs to help find bodies and a geologist to assess further risks.

It was still unclear on Wednesday how many people were buried under the mud. National Congressman Jubert Chavez Serrano, who flew to Cuzco to assess damage, told Reuters he believed 35 to 40 houses had disappeared and 150 to 200 people were missing.

Flash floods, mudslides and landslides, known locally as "huaycos", are common in Peru's Andes during the January-March rainy season. But Chavez Serrano said: "It's the worst tragedy of this kind we have seen in many years. We had some big "huaycos" 20 or 30 years ago, but never like this."
Another Congressman, Dennis Vargas Marin, who comes from the region, said 35 bodies had been found in a mudslide covering three square miles (eight square km), but that number could not be confirmed.
"Things are very bad. It's a titannic job," he said.
The tragedy comes on top of five deaths from flooding in Tamburco this weekend and three in the jungle province of Rioja where at least 750 families' homes were swept away by floods.
